exampleAnswers.title: Identifying True Statements About Sets of Vectors in a Polynomial Vector Space

question.text:
Consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_3[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $\mathbb R$ with degrees at most $3.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\big\{ t, t^2, t^3 \big\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\mathbb{R}_3[t]$
  2. $3t-2t^3$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ t, t^2, t^3 \big\}$
  3. $\big\{ t, t^2, t^3 \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}_3[t]$
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation \[ x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}t} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}t^2} + x_3 \cdot {\color{blue}t^3} = 0, \] is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=x_3=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, \[ 3t-2t^3 = 3 \cdot {\color{blue}t} + 0 \cdot {\color{blue}t^2} + (-2) \cdot {\color{blue}t^3}. \]

  • Statement III is false. For example, the polynomial $1+t$ can't be written as a linear combination of the set
    $\big\{ t, t^2, t^3 \big\}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

question.text:
Consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $\mathbb R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\big\{ 0, t, t^2 \big\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$
  2. $t^2-2t$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ 0, t, t^2 \big\}$
  3. $\big\{ 0, t, t^2 \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$
question.choice5: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. Notice that \[ 1 \cdot {\color{blue}0} + 0 \cdot {\color{blue}t} + 0 \cdot {\color{blue}t^2} = 0, \] where the first coefficient is nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent. In general, any set that contains a zero-vector is linearly dependent.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, \[ t^2-2t = 0 \cdot {\color{blue}0} + (-2) \cdot {\color{blue}t} + 1 \cdot {\color{blue}t^2}. \]

  • Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying True Statements About Sets of Vectors in a Matrix Vector Space

question.text:
Consider the vector space $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
  2. $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 8 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$
  3. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation \[ x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + x_3 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + x_4 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}}= \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \] is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=x_3=x_4=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, \[ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 8 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = 2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + (-5) \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + 8 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + 3 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, the set is linearly independent and for any matrix in $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R}),$ we get \[ \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = a\cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + b\cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + c\cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + d\cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

question.text:
Consider the vector space $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
  2. $\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$
  3. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation \[ x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \] is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, \[ \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = -2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + 5 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

  • Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ can't be written as a linear combination of \[ \bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\} \] since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry $a_{12} = 0\mathbin{:}$ \[ a \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + b \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}} = \begin{bmatrix} a &0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

  2. $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$
  3. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

Indeed, the equation \[ x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \] is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement II is false. Notice that all linear combinations of \[ \bigg\{\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}\bigg\} \] result in matrices with the entry $a_{21}=0.$

  • Statement III is false. Since the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ can't be written as a linear combination of the set, it can't form a basis.

  3. $\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}$ is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
question.explanation:

Indeed, the equation \[ x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}} + x_3 \cdot {\color{blue}\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}= \begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 \\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix} \] is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=x_3 = 0.$ So the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement III is false. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}+\mathbf{b_3} , \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is a basis of $V$
  2. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_1}+ \mathbf{b_2} \right\}$ is linearly independent
  3. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_1}+ \mathbf{b_2} \right\}$ is a basis of $V$
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

  • $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

  • $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation \begin{align*} x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2(\mathbf{b}_2+\mathbf{b}_3) + x_3\mathbf{b}_3 &= \mathbf{0} \\ \end{align*} is equivalent to \begin{align*} x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+(x_2+x_3)\mathbf{b}_3 &= \mathbf{0}, \end{align*} which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives \[ \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ x_2=0 \\ x_2+x_3=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ x_2=0 \\ x_3=0. \end{cases} \] Also, $\big\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2+\mathbf{b}_3, \mathbf{b}_3 \big\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2+\mathbf{b}_3, \mathbf{b}_3 \big\}\mathbin{:}$ \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3 = x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2(\mathbf{b}_2+\mathbf{b}_3)+(x_3-x_2)\mathbf{b}_3 \]

  • Statement II is false. Since $\mathbf{b_1}+ \mathbf{b_2} $ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{b_1}$ and $\mathbf{b_2}$, the given set is linearly dependent.

  • Statement III is false since the vector $\mathbf{b_3}$ can't be written as a linear combination of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_1}+ \mathbf{b_2} \right\}.$ But then \begin{align*} \mathbf{b_3} &=x_1 \mathbf{b}_1+x_2( \mathbf{b}_1+ \mathbf{b}_2)\\[3pt] &=(x_1 + x_2) \mathbf{b}_1+ x_2 \mathbf{b}_2, \end{align*} which would mean that $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

example.title: Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2} \big\}$ and $\mathcal{C}= \big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{c_3} \big\}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3,$ respectively.

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2} \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$
  2. $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, 2\mathbf{b_2} \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$
  3. $\big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{c_1} + \mathbf{c_2} \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

  • $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are maximally linearly independent sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3,$ respectively, and

  • $\mathcal{B}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^2,$ while $\mathcal{C}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^3.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. The set $\big\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2} \big\}$ is not a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation \begin{align*} x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2(2\mathbf{b}_2) &= \mathbf{0} \\ \end{align*} is equivalent to \begin{align*} x_1\mathbf{b}_1+(2x_2)\mathbf{b}_2 &= \mathbf{0}, \end{align*} which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}\right\}$ is linearly independent, gives \[ \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ 2x_2=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ x_2=0 . \end{cases} \] Also, $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, 2\mathbf{b_2}\big\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, 2\mathbf{b_2} \big\}\mathbin{:}$ \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2 = x_1\mathbf{b}_1+\dfrac{x_2}2\mathbf{b}_2 \]

  • Statement III is false. The set $\left\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{c_1}+\mathbf{c_2} \right\}$ is not a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ because the third vector is a linear combination of $\mathbf{c_1}$ and $\mathbf{c_2}.$ This means that the set is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

example.title: Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2} \right\}$ are bases of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\mathbb{R}^2$, respectively.

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\left\{ \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{c_1} \right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$
  2. $\left\{ -2\mathbf{b_3}, 3\mathbf{b_1}, 5\mathbf{b_2} \right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$
  3. $\left\{ \mathbf{c_1}, \mathbf{c_2}, \mathbf{x} \right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

  • $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are maximally linearly independent sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3,$ respectively, and

  • $\mathcal{B}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^2,$ while $\mathcal{C}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^3.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. The set $\big\{ \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{b}_2, \mathbf{c}_1 \big\}$ is not a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation \begin{align*} x_1(-2\mathbf{b}_3)+x_2(3\mathbf{b}_1)+x_3(5\mathbf{b}_2) &= \mathbf{0} \\ \end{align*} is equivalent to \begin{align*} (-2x_1)\mathbf{b}_3+(3x_2)\mathbf{b}_1+(5x_3)\mathbf{b}_2 &= \mathbf{0}, \end{align*} which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives \[ \begin{cases} -2x_1= 0\\ 3x_2=0 \\ 5x_3=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ x_2=0 \\ x_3=0. \end{cases} \] Also, $\big\{ -2\mathbf{b}_3, 3\mathbf{b}_1, 5\mathbf{b}_2 \big\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ -2\mathbf{b}_3, 3\mathbf{b}_1, 5\mathbf{b}_2 \big\}\mathbin{:}$ \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3 = \dfrac{x_1}{3}(3\mathbf{b}_1)+\dfrac{x_2}{5}(5\mathbf{b}_2)+\left(-\dfrac{x_3}{2}\right)(-2\mathbf{b}_3) \]

  • Statement III is false. Since $\mathcal{C}= \big\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb R^2$, any vector of $\mathbb{R}^2,$ including the given vector $\mathbf{x},$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{c}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2.$ This means that $\big\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2, \mathbf{x} \big\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

question.text:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \big\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2} \big\}$ is linearly independent
  2. $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{w} \big\}$ is linearly independent
  3. $\big\{ 2\mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \big\}$ is a basis of $V$
question.choice5: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

  • $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

  • $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, if $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2} \big\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2=\mathbf{0}, \] where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+0\mathbf{b}_3=\mathbf{0}, \] which would mean that $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis.

  • Statement II is false. Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent.

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation \begin{align*} x_1(2\mathbf{b}_1)+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3 &= \mathbf{0} \\ \end{align*} is equivalent to \begin{align*} (2x_1)\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3 &= \mathbf{0}, \end{align*} which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives \[ \begin{cases} 2x_1= 0\\ x_2=0 \\ x_3=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ x_2=0 \\ x_3=0. \end{cases} \] Also, $\big\{ 2\mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \big\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ 2\mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \big\}\mathbin{:}$ \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3 = \dfrac{x_1}{2}(2\mathbf{b}_1)+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3 \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

example.title: Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \big\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\big\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \big\}$ is linearly independent
  2. $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{w} \big\}$ is a basis of $V$
  3. $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_1} + \mathbf{b_3} \big\}$ is linearly independent
question.explanation:
Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

  • $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

  • $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, if $\big\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \big\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_2+x_2\mathbf{b}_3=\mathbf{0}, \] where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+0\mathbf{b}_3=\mathbf{0}, \] which would mean that $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis.

  • Statement II is false. Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent. Hence, the given set is not a basis for $V.$

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation \begin{align*} x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3(\mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_3) &= \mathbf{0} \\ \end{align*} is equivalent to \begin{align*} (x_1+x_3)\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3 &= \mathbf{0}, \end{align*} which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives \[ \begin{cases} x_1+x_3= 0\\ x_2=0 \\ x_3=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1= 0\\ x_2=0 \\ x_3=0. \end{cases} \] Also, $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b_3} \big\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b_3} \big\}\mathbin{:}$ \[ x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3 = (x_1-x_3)\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3(\mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_3) \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."
